title: What the long story teaches
hook: faith kept through exile, loss and renewal

segments.voice: Yesterday, pangat, and your line was tens of thousands fed. Today, a step back from the kitchen to look at the whole year's road.

Stand at the end of a long road and look back, and you can't see every step. You see the shape. A man with a musician beside him, walking from village to village. Towns built around a pool and a kitchen. Gurus who gave their lives rather than give way. A morning when five stood up. Hard years in the hills and forests. A kingdom won and lost. Marches with no weapons. A land split in two. A temple attacked, and grief in the streets. Families scattered across oceans, building gurdwaras in rented halls.
screen: `A MAN AND A MUSICIAN, WALKING.` → `MARTYRS, MARCHES, A LAND SPLIT.` → `GURDWARAS IN RENTED HALLS.`

segments.voice: The losses are real, and this story doesn't pretend. There were Gurus tortured and killed, families driven from their homes, sacred places damaged, and friends who never came back. Sikhs say those names out loud. In the Ardas, the prayer said standing at the close of Sikh services, the sangat recalls those who gave their lives and kept their faith: who were cut limb from limb, broken on wheels, sawn apart, and who kept their Sikhi with their uncut hair to the last breath. The losses are carried, standing, every day. And after every hard chapter, something kept going. The Granth kept being read. The kitchen kept cooking. The gurdwara door kept opening, in a village in Punjab, a river town in Malaysia, a rented hall in a northern winter. Sikhs often tell it this way: the faith didn't go on by winning every fight, but by keeping its daily practices. The Ardas ends with this line: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. Through the Name, rising spirits, and by your will, the good of all. Chardi kala is the word for that spirit: rising, steady, even in loss. And notice what it asks for at the very end. Not victory. The good of all. As the Ardas holds it: remember everything, keep the practice, and keep asking good for everyone.
screen: `THE LOSSES ARE REAL.` · `THE ARDAS REMEMBERS THEM.` · `THE KITCHEN KEPT COOKING.` · `CHARDI KALA, AND THE GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `THE LESSON OF THE STORY.`

segments.voice: Let the year's stories pass in front of you like a slow train, the musician, the five, the marches, the kitchens, without holding on to any of them. Let one stop, the one that stayed with you most, and as you breathe out, name quietly one thing it taught you. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Chardi kala. Rising spirits, the steady, hopeful spirit asked for through the Name, kept through a faith's exile, loss and renewal. Today's word.
Your line: the lesson of the story. One lesson, named, is plenty. That's day one thousand forty-four.

chat.says: After so much loss in Sikh history, what does the Ardas end by asking for?
options: Chardi kala, rising spirits through the Name, and sarbat da bhala, the good of all.
Victory over every enemy, so that the losses of the past are finally repaid.
Only the safety of the Sikh community itself, before anyone else's good.
